clue.text: Justify precious landscape painter

parts.note: to aver is to assert or vindicate, so justify gives aver
affectedly precious behaviour is camp

explanation.surface: Someone defends a painter's dainty, over-refined landscapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Precious' here means affected or mannered, the sense of camp. Hendrick Avercamp was a Dutch painter of winter landscapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hendrick Avercamp was a seventeenth-century Dutch artist famous for frozen winter scenes, a painter of landscapes.

clue.text: Very old record one put on for foxy character

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient disc with one track added is played for a cunning person.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's play takes its name from its title character, whose name is Italian for 'old fox'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's schemer is named after the fox, the emblem of cunning, so he is the foxy character.

clue.text: Hope inspired, idealistically romantic

parts.note: the novelist Anthony Hope invented this imaginary kingdom for The Prisoner of Zenda, and it now stands for any idealistically romantic setting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' looks like the feeling, but it is Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda; the land he dreamt up gave English an adjective for romantic, swashbuckling fantasy.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional Central European kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda, created by Anthony Hope, symbolises idealised romance and intrigue.

clue.text: Novel heroine from the Middle East, inter alia

indicators.note: to inter is to bury, so the Middle East letters are buried within the word alia

explanation.surface: A fictional heroine hails from the Middle East, among other places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inter alia' reads as the Latin phrase for 'among other things', but 'inter' is the verb meaning bury. Henry Fielding's last novel is named after its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia Booth is the title heroine of Henry Fielding's 1751 novel Amelia.

clue.text: Caused by Master's comic gift?

parts.note: Noel Coward was nicknamed the Master; his comic gift causes merriment in the audience right now, which names one of his comedies

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Master' was Noel Coward's nickname. Read literally, the clue describes the amusement his talent produces in the moment; that phrase is also the title of his 1939 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's play about the actor Garry Essendine carries this title, and the phrase also describes mirth occurring now.

clue.text: Namely poor, and backward, nevertheless a name featuring in four of the Histories

definitions.text: a name featuring in four of the Histories

parts.note: SC abbreviates scilicet, Latin for namely

indicators.note: the word poor is to be read backward, right to left

explanation.surface: A sentence about someone poor and slow who still turns up in several Shakespeare history plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' looks like a description of the poor person, but it turns POOR into ROOP. Lord Scroop (or Scrope) appears in Richard II, both parts of Henry IV and Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Scroop is a family surname borne by characters such as the Archbishop of York and Lord Scroop of Masham in Shakespeare's histories.

clue.text: Girl supports second friend for composer

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath, so the girl's name goes below the others

parts.note: a chum is a friend
Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman props up her closest friend's runner-up in a music contest.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'supports' means the girl's name is written below the rest. Robert Schumann married the pianist Clara Wieck.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Schumann was a German Romantic who wrote symphonies, piano works and songs.

clue.text: Sort of theatre misused in opera

indicators.note: letters that are misused are put into the wrong arrangement, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some kind of stage space is being abused in an operatic production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misused' rearranges IN OPERA into OPEN AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-air theatre is a kind of venue performed under the sky rather than indoors.

clue.text: Undisciplined Leone epic: a sort of prehistoric Western, perhaps?

definitions.text: a sort of prehistoric Western, perhaps?

indicators.note: something undisciplined is out of order, so the letters of the director's name and the film word are jumbled

explanation.surface: Sergio Leone's sprawling film is a wild Western set in ancient times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undisciplined' rearranges LEONE EPIC. Leone was known for spaghetti Westerns, so a film set in this geological epoch would be a prehistoric Western.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pliocene, also spelt Pleiocene, is a geological epoch millions of years ago, so it is a prehistoric period.

clue.text: Rumoured pilgrim science-fiction writer

indicators.note: something rumoured is spoken of, signalling that a word is said aloud

parts.note: the Clerk of Oxford is one of Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims

explanation.surface: Word gets around that a pilgrim writes science fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'clerk' is pronounced 'clark'. Arthur C. Clarke wrote 2001: A Space Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur C. Clarke was a British author of novels such as Childhood's End, works of science fiction.

clue.text: Playwright gives point there, to good English

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dramatist makes his point to a fine Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' is a compass point, here E for east. George Etherege wrote Restoration comedies such as The Man of Mode.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir George Etherege was a Restoration dramatist whose comedies include The Man of Mode.

clue.text: I interrupt German poet to indicate French fabulist

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so the letter I breaks into the German's name

parts.note: Theodor Fontane was a German poet and novelist

explanation.surface: Someone cuts into a German poet's work to point out a French storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: Theodor Fontane wrote ballads as well as novels such as Effi Briest; adding I gives Fontaine, as in Jean de La Fontaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean de La Fontaine wrote the Fables, verse tales with animal characters, making him a fabulist.

clue.text: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"

definitions.text: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"

parts.words: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"
parts.note: a line from Gilbert and Sullivan with one word missing after humane; the missing word is the emperor's title and the opera's name

explanation.walkthrough: The line is the emperor's entrance song in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera set in Japan; the solver supplies the title the song omits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese emperor in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera sings this line about himself, and his title is the missing word.

clue.text: Far-seeing novelist, never translated

indicators.note: translated means changed into another form, so the letters of the word never are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A visionary author whose works have never appeared in other languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' rearranges NEVER. Jules Verne foresaw submarines and space travel, hence far-seeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne wrote prophetic adventures like Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, anticipating later technology.

clue.text: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me" (Charles Lamb)

definitions.text: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me" (Charles Lamb)

parts.words: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me"
parts.note: Lamb describes seeing a ghostly clerk pass him, the kind of imagined apparition that marks someone given to fanciful sights

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation comes from Lamb's Essays of Elia, where the narrator pictures the ghosts of old clerks; such fancies belong to a dreamer who sees things.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sees phantoms and imaginary figures is a seer of things unseen by others, a dreamer.

clue.text: Reseating arrangement for Hornung piece

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things in a new order, so the letters of reseating are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rearranging the seats is a fresh setting of a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges RESEATING. E. W. Hornung, creator of Raffles, also wrote Stingaree, about an Australian bushranger.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingaree (1905) is a collection of stories by E. W. Hornung about a gentleman outlaw, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Excellent as Barrie's butler

definitions.meaning: J. M. Barrie's play about Crichton, the butler who takes charge on a desert island, gives him this epithet

explanation.walkthrough: 'as' links the two senses. Barrie's play is The Admirable Crichton.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means wonderful, praiseworthy; it is also the epithet of Crichton, the butler in Barrie's comedy.

clue.text: Gothic stepdame in unseemly rush

indicators.note: Gothic in the sense of barbarous and crude signals the letters of stepdame being rudely jumbled

explanation.surface: A wicked stepmother of Gothic fiction is caught in an undignified dash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gothic' looks like it describes the stepmother of horror fiction, but it rearranges STEPDAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong charge, often panicked, a disorderly dash.

clue.text: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford

definitions.text: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford

parts.words: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford
parts.note: Aloysius is not a student but the teddy bear carried by Lord Flyte in Waugh's Brideshead Revisited

explanation.walkthrough: Aloysius sounds like a fellow undergraduate, but it is the teddy bear of Sebastian Flyte in Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebastian Flyte keeps a teddy bear called Aloysius in his rooms at Oxford in Brideshead Revisited.

clue.text: Country musician heard

indicators.note: heard signals that the composer's name is spoken aloud

parts.note: Benjamin Britten was an English composer

explanation.surface: A country-music performer is being listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like country music, but it is the definition. Benjamin Britten's surname sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain is the island nation comprising England, Scotland and Wales.

clue.text: Tickle Calliope, for example ()

definitions.meaning: to tickle someone is to entertain or divert them
Calliope is one of the nine Greek goddesses of the arts, so she is one such goddess

explanation.walkthrough: The empty brackets mark the second reading as two words, A MUSE: Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: To tickle is to make someone laugh, which is entertaining them; and Calliope is one of the nine Muses.

clue.text: Coningsby's role model gets first-class return to port

parts.note: Sidon is an ancient Phoenician port in Lebanon

indicators.note: the first-class letters return, being read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here as AI

explanation.surface: Someone gets a first-class trip back to harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, written AI, means first-class; 'return' turns it to IA. In Disraeli's novel Coningsby, the wise Sidonia guides the young hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidonia is the worldly mentor whom the hero of Disraeli's novel Coningsby looks up to.

clue.text: Uninteresting publicity for spirits

parts.note: dry means dull or uninteresting
ads are advertisements, publicity

explanation.walkthrough: 'spirits' suggests alcohol, fitting 'dry' and publicity, but means tree nymphs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are tree nymphs of Greek myth, nature spirits.

clue.text: Sash from 12 is medieval black magic

parts.note: 12 across is set in Japan, where the obi is the sash worn with a kimono
taken as written
M is an abbreviation for medieval

explanation.surface: A Japanese sash turns out to be an instrument of dark sorcery.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' points to the answer at 12 across, set in Japan, whose sash is the OBI. Obiism, or obeah, is Caribbean sorcery.
explanation.definitionFit: Obiism, a form of obeah, is witchcraft or sorcery practised in the West Indies, so it is dark magic.

clue.text: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her

definitions.text: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her

parts.words: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her
parts.note: the dying queen in Hamlet cries out that the drink has poisoned her, so the drink killed her rather than made her drunk

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a confessed drinker, but the queen in Hamlet drinks the poisoned cup meant for her son and cries 'The drink, the drink!'
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's mother, the queen, dies from drinking the poisoned wine prepared by Claudius.

clue.text: Foot of a peasant fractured

indicators.note: something fractured is broken up, so the letters of a peasant are rearranged

explanation.surface: A farm labourer has broken his foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' looks like the body part, but it is a metrical foot; 'fractured' rearranges A PEASANT.
explanation.definitionFit: An anapaest is a metrical foot of two short syllables followed by a long one.

clue.text: Some attached to vestment in ancient kingdom

indicators.note: attached to puts the word for some right after the vestment

parts.note: an alb is a white liturgical vestment
any means some

explanation.surface: A few people are attached to their robes in a historic realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attached to' joins the second piece on after the vestment. Albany, the old name for northern Scotland, survives in the ducal title Duke of Albany.
explanation.definitionFit: Albany, or Alba, was the old Celtic kingdom of northern Britain, later Scotland, a realm of antiquity.

clue.text: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot

definitions.text: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot

parts.words: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot
parts.note: Mark Twain's novel sends a man from Connecticut back to King Arthur's court

explanation.walkthrough: Twain's novel is A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court, where an American is transported to Camelot.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's time-travelling hero is a New Englander, an American from Connecticut, at Arthur's court.

clue.text: Princely refugee from Happy Valley

parts.note: Samuel Johnson's Abyssinian prince escapes the secluded paradise where royal children are kept

explanation.walkthrough: In Johnson's tale, an Abyssinian prince flees the enclosed Happy Valley to seek happiness in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's novel The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia, follows the prince who escapes the Happy Valley.
